Lepton is an Android compatibility layer for Linux developed by Valve Corporation. It is based on Waydroid and allows Android applications to run on SteamOS and other Linux-based operating systems. It is comparable to Valve's Proton, which provides Microsoft Windows application compatibility on Linux, but targets Android instead.
Lepton was developed for the Steam Frame, Valve's standalone virtual reality headset, which runs SteamOS on ARM-based hardware. The layer allows the headset to run VR applications that were built for Android-based devices such as Meta Quest.
Background
Several virtual reality headsets, including the Meta Quest series, run Android and use applications built for that operating system. The Steam Frame, announced in November 2025, runs SteamOS rather than Android, which meant existing Android VR applications could not run on it without a compatibility layer.
Valve had previously developed Proton, a fork of Wine, to run Windows games on Linux. Proton is used on the Steam Deck. Lepton takes a similar approach, forking the open-source Waydroid project rather than building a new Android compatibility solution.
Technical overview
Lepton is based on Waydroid, which runs Android inside a Linux namespace container. Waydroid uses a system image derived from LineageOS and requires the Wayland display protocol.
The containerization approach differs from full emulation or virtualization in that Android applications can access host hardware directly while remaining isolated from the host operating system. Applications must be compiled for the same CPU architecture as the host device, or use additional translation layers.
The Steam Frame uses an ARM-based Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 processor, so Lepton can run ARM64 Android applications without translation on that device. On x86-based systems such as the Steam Deck, ARM-only Android applications would require additional translation.
Development
Reports of Valve experimenting with Waydroid appeared in 2024. The name "Lepton" was identified in December 2025 through listings on SteamDB, a third-party database that tracks Steam applications. The listings included a main application and a development version, with a logo depicting a frog.
The name follows Valve's convention of naming compatibility software after subatomic particles.
Compatibility testing lists on SteamDB showed that Valve had tested Android VR applications including Moss Book II, Open Brush, Pistol Whip, and The Lab.
Use on Steam Frame
The Steam Frame is Valve's first device to run SteamOS on ARM architecture. It uses three compatibility layers: Proton for Windows games, FEX-Emu for x86-to-ARM instruction translation, and Lepton for Android applications.
